title: Expired Certificate: What to Do?
context: An internal site presents an expired self-signed certificate. Users see a warning and some are bypassing the control.

n1.text: First action before making any renewal decision?

choices.text: Disable certificate verification in the browser
choices.why: Disabling validation removes the control and exposes users to on-path attacks.

choices.text: Identify the certificate owner and the trust chain
choices.why: You must first know who issues it, who holds the private key, and whether the CA is trusted.

choices.text: Replace the certificate with a shared symmetric key
choices.why: A symmetric key does not provide server authentication via a certificate.

n2.text: The certificate must be replaced with a third-party CA certificate. Which step comes before issuance?

choices.text: Generate a CSR and send the private key to the CA
choices.why: The private key never leaves the server: only the CSR is sent.

choices.text: Generate a CSR on the server and keep the private key locally
choices.why: The CSR contains the public key; the private key stays on the server.

choices.text: Purchase a new private key from the CA
choices.why: A CA does not provide your private key.

n3.text: How can you quickly verify that a revoked certificate is no longer accepted?

choices.why: CRL (list) and OCSP (online query) are the two certificate revocation checking mechanisms.
Disk encryption has no connection to certificate revocation.

n4.outcome: You followed the chain: owner → CSR → local private key → CRL/OCSP verification.

debrief: The private key must never be transmitted to the CA.
CSR = certificate signing request containing the public key.
CRL and OCSP check revocation; a self-signed certificate does not provide third-party trust.
